hook.speaker: Arjuna
hook.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
hook.sanskrit: न चैतद्विद्मः कतरन्नो गरीयोयद्वा जयेम यदि वा नो जयेयुः । यानेव हत्वा न जिजीविषामस्तेऽवस्थिताः प्रमुखे धार्तराष्ट्राः ॥
hook.line: I can't tell which is better, or even what winning would look like.
hook.translation: Nor do we know which is better for us, to fight or not, or whether we will win or they will. The very people after whose death we would not wish to live stand facing us.
hook.why: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

verse.meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield and looks at the people he must fight. He does not know which choice is right. He cannot tell if fighting or staying is better. He does not know if they will win or lose. He feels that even if they win, he would not want to live after killing these people. He admits he is lost. He asks Krishna to teach him.
verse.for_you: You are standing at a crossroads where neither path feels clear. You do not know if leaving your work is the right move or if staying is the right move. You are afraid of what comes next, and that fear is heavy.
verse.try_today: Notice when your mind races ahead to the worst possible outcome.
verse.scene_line: You are on your own battlefield, looking at the people you love and not knowing which way to turn.
asks: How do I ask for help when I am supposed to have the answers?
What does it mean to admit I do not know?
Can I stay in this uncertainty without falling apart?

verse.speaker: Vishnu
verse.setting: Vishnu explains to the frightened gods where fear comes from.
verse.sanskrit: दीनताजं भयं माने गुणे खलभयं खलु । भयं निन्दकजं शक्तौ विद्यायां वादिनं भयम् ॥
verse.line: Honour fears disgrace, virtue fears the wicked, power fears critics, learning fears debate. Every gain brings a fear.
verse.translation: In honour lies the fear of being brought low; in virtue, the fear of the wicked; in power, the fear of critics; in learning, the fear of rival debaters.
verse.why: Every gain brings its own fear; holding things lightly is the way out.

prasang.title: Vishnu on where fear comes from
prasang.summary: The frightened gods ask Vishnu how to become fearless. He explains that every possession carries its own fear (the body fears age, wealth fears thieves, power fears critics) and that only dispassion is free of fear; then he restates Bhagavad Gita 2.14-15 on enduring pleasure and pain.
prasang.lesson: Every gain brings its own fear; holding things lightly is the way out.

verse.meaning: The frightened gods ask Vishnu how to become fearless. He answers that fear is the price of every gain. Honour brings the fear of disgrace. Virtue brings the fear of the wicked. Power brings the fear of critics. Learning brings the fear of rival debaters. Every possession carries its own danger. The only way out is to hold things lightly.
verse.for_you: You are caught between keeping your job or walking away, and the fear of what comes next. This verse names the trap you are in. You are trying to secure your family's future by controlling the outcome, but every gain brings its own fear.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment where you try to control an outcome today.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own kitchen, holding a cup of tea, and the fear of what comes next is the only thing you are holding.
asks: What if I let go of the outcome today?
How do I hold my work lightly?
What is the fear that comes with my gain?

verse.speaker: Tulsidas
verse.setting: Frightened by hard times, Tulsidas asks Ram to say the words he needs to hear.
verse.sanskrit: रीति सुनि रावरी प्रतीति-प्रीति रावरे सों, डरत हौं देखि कलिकालको कहरु। कहेही बनैगी कै कहाये, बलि जाउँ, राम, “तुलसी ! तू मेरो, हारि हिये न हहरु'॥
verse.line: "You are mine. Do not lose heart, do not tremble."
verse.translation: Having heard your ways, my trust and love are in you, yet I am afraid, seeing the cruelty of these times. It will only be well if you say it, or have it said, Ram: "Tulsi, you are mine. Do not lose heart, do not tremble."

verse.meaning: Frightened by the cruelty of these times, Tulsidas turns to Ram. He says his trust and love are in Ram, yet he is afraid. He asks Ram to say the words that will hold him steady. Ram replies, 'You are mine. Do not lose heart, do not tremble.' verse offers a promise of belonging as the answer to fear.
verse.for_you: You are standing in the middle of a choice that feels too large to hold, and your mind is already living through the worst of it. Tulsidas was afraid too, but he was also held. The work you do and the people you care for are yours.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment where you are held, not where you might fall.

verse.speaker: Yama
verse.setting: Yama on the self within changing bodies.
verse.sanskrit: अशरीरँ शरीरेष्वनवस्थेष्ववस्थितम् । महान्तं विभुमात्मानं मत्वा धीरो न शोचति ॥
verse.line: Knowing what stays steady inside all that changes, the wise do not grieve.
verse.translation: Knowing the self as bodiless within bodies, steady among the unsteady, great and all-pervading, the wise one does not grieve.
verse.why: What you most are cannot be lost, and a quiet, honest life is how you find it.

prasang.title: Yama on what does not die
prasang.summary: Death himself explains that the true self is never born and never dies, and is not killed when the body is. It is found not by cleverness or study but by a calm, honest life.
prasang.lesson: What you most are cannot be lost, and a quiet, honest life is how you find it.

verse.meaning: Yama is teaching Nachiketa about the self that lives inside the body and outlives it. He says the true self is not born and does not die. It is not cut down when the body is cut. It is bodiless, steady, and all-pervading. Knowing this, the wise one does not grieve.
verse.for_you: Your mind is rehearsing futures that have not happened. The work you do, the care you give, the children you are raising, they all rest on something that cannot be lost. That steady core is what stays when the plans change.
verse.scene_line: You are inside the changing body, waiting for the steady self to show itself.

verse.setting: The sage Vasishtha to Bharat, shattered by his father's death and Ram's exile.
verse.sanskrit: तात हृदयँ धीरजु धरहु करहु जो अवसर आजु। उठे भरत गुर बचन सुनि करन कहेउ सबु साजु ॥
verse.line: Keep courage in your heart, and do what today asks of you.
verse.translation: "Child, keep courage in your heart, and do what this moment asks of you today." Hearing his teacher, Bharat rose and had everything made ready.
verse.why: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

prasang.title: Bharat refuses the throne
prasang.summary: After the funeral, Vasishtha, the ministers and Kausalya all urge Bharat to rule, as his father wished. Bharat says the advice is right and his heart still isn't at peace; the crown means nothing without Ram. He decides to go to the forest, admit his fault, and trust his brother to forgive.
prasang.story_hook: Everyone agreed the throne was his, and Bharat could not bring himself to sit on it.
prasang.lesson: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha speaks to Bharat, who is broken after his father's death and his brother's exile. Bharat wants to give the throne up and go to the forest to beg for forgiveness. Vasishtha tells him to keep courage in his heart and do what this moment asks. Bharat rises and gets everything ready to leave. The verse asks you to stop living in the future and simply meet the task in front of you.
verse.for_you: You are caught between staying and leaving, and the unknown is eating at you. Vasishtha tells Bharat to stop weighing the crown and simply do what the moment asks. In your own quiet, do what this hour asks of you.
verse.try_today: Name the single task waiting for you right now.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the edge of the forest, ready to do what this moment asks.
asks: What is the very next task I can do today?
How do I keep courage when I feel I have wronged them?
What does doing what today asks look like for me?

verse.speaker: Narrator
verse.setting: Ram, standing before Shiva's bow, sees Sita's anguish and knows the moment won't wait.
verse.sanskrit: देखी बिपुल बिकल बैदेही। निमिष बिहात कलप सम तेही। तृषित बारि बिनु जो तनु त्यागा। मुएँ करइ का सुधा तड़ागा ॥ का बरषा सब कृषी सुखानें। समय चुकें पुनि का पछितानें॥ अस जियँ जानि जानकी देखी। प्रभु पुलके लखि प्रीति बिसेषी ॥
verse.line: What use is rain after the crops have dried? Act while the moment is still here.
verse.translation: He saw Vaidehi in deep distress, each moment passing like an age. If a thirsty man dies for want of water, what use is a lake of nectar after he is gone? What use is rain when the crops have dried? What use is regret once the moment has passed? Knowing this, he looked at Janaki, and seeing her deep love, he thrilled.
verse.why: Some moments do not wait; when it is time, act.

prasang.title: Janaka's despair and the bow
prasang.summary: Ten thousand kings fail to lift Shiva's bow, and Janaka cries out that the earth has no heroes left. Lakshman bristles; Vishwamitra sends Ram forward. Ram sees Sita's anguish, knows that rain after the crops have dried is useless, lifts the bow and breaks it in a moment.
prasang.story_hook: Ten thousand kings had tried the bow, and the room had gone quiet.
prasang.lesson: Some moments do not wait; when it is time, act.

verse.meaning: The narrator asks the reader to consider a man who has died of thirst. A lake of nectar and a downpour of rain cannot help him now. The moment has passed. The point is that some moments do not wait for our readiness. When the time is here, action is the only answer, because regret after the moment is useless.
verse.for_you: You are standing at a moment that will not wait. The mind imagines a thousand futures, but the present is already here. The question is not what might happen, but what today asks of you. Let the next move be small and real.
verse.try_today: Ask what this exact moment asks of you, and do that one thing.
verse.scene_line: You are at the moment that will not wait, with a choice that cannot be put off.
asks: What does this exact moment ask of me?
How do I stop waiting for a better feeling to act?
What is the smallest move I can make right now?

story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

anchor.speaker: Janaka
anchor.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
anchor.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
anchor.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
anchor.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
anchor.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
anchor.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.
